candidates.title: COVERAGE-TRACE: Source-Side Counterfactual Tracing for Detecting Omissions in LLM Summaries
candidates.abstract: Omissions are difficult to verify because missing information leaves no output span to inspect: a summary may be factually supported while still excluding a decision, qualification, quantity, or condition needed to preserve the source's meaning. We introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual framework that evaluates omission as dependence on a designated atomic source fact. It replaces only the target fact with type-matched alternatives, holds the candidate summary fixed, and measures the resulting change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. A summary covering the target should respond more strongly than one omitting it, while aggregation across multiple counterfactuals reduces sensitivity to replacement choice. We evaluate COVERAGE-TRACE on 80 matched covered--omitted QMSum pairs spanning several fact types and four open-weight models. Multi-CF achieves 0.764--0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest evaluated text-only baseline. On Falcon-7B, targeted interventions achieve 0.779 AUROC, whereas shuffling counterfactual assignments reduces performance to 0.533; target deletion is effective while unrelated deletion is not. However, adjustment for meaning-preserving paraphrases reduces AUROC to 0.591--0.624. COVERAGE-TRACE therefore provides a practical, complementary signal of target-specific source--summary dependence, but not a wording-invariant semantic coverage probability. These results establish source-side intervention as a promising approach to omission detection while identifying semantic invariance as the central remaining challenge.

candidates.title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video
candidates.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. candidates.title: VidToC: Rethinking Video Token Compression for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.

candidates.title: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. candidates.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
candidates.abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

candidates.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

candidates.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
candidates.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

candidates.title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
candidates.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

candidates.title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators

We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. candidates.title: Cyber-Physical RSI for AI-RAN: A Case Study
candidates.abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.

candidates.title: MambaLIFT: Reference-Based Mechanism-Aware Attribution for VMamba
candidates.abstract: Attributing predictions of visual state-space models remains challenging because input-dependent selective dynamics couple feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared computational pathways. MambaLIFT decomposes the reference-relative class-logit difference, \(f_c(x)-f_c(x^0)\), by spatial position, VSS block, scan direction, and computational mechanism. Experiments on ImageNet-1K evaluate VMamba-T and VMamba-B, with hyperparameters selected on a calibration set and faithfulness assessed on a disjoint held-out evaluation set. MambaLIFT achieves numerical conservation to floating-point precision across audited attribution interfaces in both configurations. Under mean-colour pixel flipping, it achieves significantly higher mean faithfulness scores than MambaLRP on both configurations and the highest scores among the evaluated methods, including Integrated Gradients with matched references. Under blurred replacement, MambaLIFT is non-inferior to MambaLRP on VMamba-T and equivalent on VMamba-B, indicating that its advantage depends on the replacement protocol. Ablations on VMamba-T show that interaction allocation, temporal propagation, and pathway composition affect attribution maps. Mechanism-level analyses further show that exact relevance conservation does not imply additive effects under finite interventions: the mechanism decomposition accounts for the reference-relative logit difference but does not estimate intervention effects or establish causal validity.

candidates.title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
candidates.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.

candidates.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
candidates.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.

candidates.title: Calibrate in Context: Efficient Data-Free Quantization from Small Synthetic Pools
candidates.abstract: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.

candidates.title: Interpreting DeepStack-Style Vision-Language Models: Do Input or Deeper-Layer Visual Tokens Drive Answers?
candidates.abstract: DeepStack-style vision-language models feed visual tokens to the language model at its input, and again at deeper layers. We call these the main entry and the later entries. What do the later entries add when the model already has the image? We give the entries versions that differ in one object's color and see which one the answer follows. On photographs, the original DeepStack follows the later entries, while Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follow the main entry. Does weakening the main entry give the later features more influence? On synthetic images, we keep this conflict and reduce color saturation at the main entry only. The unchanged later features gain a stronger effect on the relative scores of the two colors, in all four models, including Granite Vision. This holds even under mild desaturation, when accuracy without the conflict stays at 100%. To test whether later features can also correct errors, we degrade both entries and restore only the later ones. The same blur costs both Qwen models 50 percentage points of accuracy on stripe orientation. The 32B model recovers 48 points and the 8B model only 8. Accuracy with one clean entry predicted which entry each model can lose, and five of six tested predictions held on new GQA attribute questions. With the other entry zeroed, Qwen3-VL-8B loses only 0.3 points on its main entry alone, and DeepStack at most 3.45 points on either entry alone. In split inference on these questions, DeepStack can then send only its main-entry features at higher precision. This takes 49% fewer bytes than all entries at a shared precision, at similar accuracy.

candidates.title: Mitigating Row Buffer Contention Through Multiple Row Buffer (MRB) DRAM
candidates.abstract: DRAM chips contain multiple banks to handle sev- eral memory requests in parallel. However, requests to different rows of the same bank (e.g., from different cores or workload access patterns) interfere with each other by contending for a single shared row buffer. This introduces row buffer conflicts, which incur performance and energy overheads. In this work, we reduce row buffer conflicts caused by interference by introducing multiple row buffers in each bank. We propose multiple row buffer (MRB) DRAM, which employs a primary global row buffer along with multiple secondary SRAM row buffers in the DRAM chip. These secondary SRAM row buffers act as a cache that enables each bank to serve requests to multiple rows in parallel, thereby improving performance and reducing row buffer conflicts. Our evaluation shows that MRB-DRAM with four SRBs per bank improves performance by an average of 29.7%, 24% in singlecore, multicore systems, respectively, compared to a conventional DDR4 baseline with a modest area overhead of 2%.

candidates.title: VR-SparseQuant: Accurate FP4 Quantization with 2:4 Sparsity on Vera Rubin
candidates.abstract: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors. Offline scale-ratio calibration avoids runtime search, while a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams efficiently. On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from $\boldsymbol{6.85}$ to $\boldsymbol{5.57}$ versus dense RTN W4A4. Including activation preparation, our native Rubin kernels for VRFP4 achieve up to $\boldsymbol{3.1\times}$ GEMM and $\boldsymbol{2.7\times}$ MoE speedup over BF16. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of adaptive activation quantization using Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions.

candidates.title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
candidates.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA

candidates.title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
candidates.abstract: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.

candidates.title: Can LLMs Resolve Entity Conflicts in Domain Specific NLU Pipelines?
candidates.abstract: Resolving entity conflicts is a critical step in Pipeline-based NLU architectures, especially when multiple extractors provide overlapping or conflicting outputs. Traditional rule-based entity conflict resolution methods often lack flexibility and are unscalable. In this work, we aim to study if the broad knowledge of LLMs can be leveraged to resolve entity conflicts in domain specific NLU pipelines. We present an experimental comparison between a traditional rule-based conflict resolution method, and two LLM-based approaches: a multi-shot prompting method using the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model and a LoRA fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model. The evaluation was conducted under two setups: (1) a broad assessment of LLM's capability to match existing NLU pipeline output, and (2) a more controlled scenario assessing the LLM accuracy on human-labeled data. Results show that while multi-shot prompting offers ease of adaptation and rapid behavioral changes, the fine-tuned model delivers superior performance on complex, ambiguous cases. Ultimately, the best approach appears to be a combination of both strategies, leveraging multi-shot prompting's flexibility alongside the broad accuracy gains of LoRA fine-tuning for a more comprehensive performance.

candidates.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
candidates.abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer-agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, 37.24% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains 93.06% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

candidates.title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
candidates.abstract: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from the words of a sentence, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads it. We study how much of prominence language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. On read English speech labelled for word-level prominence, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. All text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and largely make the same errors. With the prompts we tested, LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. Linear probes find more in their representations. Speech models reach 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of prominence, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting does not bring it out: they represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell you.

candidates.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
candidates.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.

candidates.title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
candidates.abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.

candidates.title: Self-Replicating Language Models
candidates.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are a form of life is a scientifically interesting question. Under the Darwinian definition of life, it is also a practical one, because a system capable of Darwinian Evolution can adapt. We therefore test several modes in which a language model can reproduce itself: by emitting a genome that trains its offspring, by copying and mutating its own weights, and by teaching a child from its own samples. In principle, small language models can replicate and evolve: selection improves them, and they adapt to narrow niches. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model, unlike any organism, can lower its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship LLMs can write such replicators, but for a large LLM to replicate by teaching its offspring remains, for now, technically and economically infeasible.

candidates.title: TableRoute: Capability-Aware Routing for Scalable Table Question Answering
candidates.abstract: Table question answering with large language models remains difficult to scale: tables range from compact to million-token sizes, while questions require precise grounding of columns, values, and computations. Existing methods often specialize in a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across different table scales and model capabilities. Full-table reading is efficient for compact inputs but suffers from irrelevant context. Table reduction helps long inputs but depends on reliable evidence localization, while execution is required when tables exceed the model context window and remains sensitive to schema and value grounding errors. We propose TableRoute, a capability-aware routing framework with evidence-conditioned inference for scalable TableQA. TableRoute first generates validated question--table evidence and identifies the required operations, then routes each instance among these three strategies according to serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles these operations. The validated evidence supports the selected route by grounding columns, values, and conditions. Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales, while reducing online token cost. Code will be made available upon publication.

candidates.title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
candidates.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.

candidates.title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
candidates.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.

candidates.title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
candidates.abstract: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.

candidates.title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
candidates.abstract: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.

candidates.title: The Linguistic Structure of Dependency-Conditioned Embeddings
candidates.abstract: Dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, but the geometric organisation of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored. We investigate the global and local geometry of lemma-dependency relation embeddings using 4 representations trained on WikiText-103: 2 count-based PPMI configurations and 2 Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) configurations. At the global level, we analyse dependency-relation centroids, control for lexical identity through within-lemma centring, and examine their alignment with part-of-speech (POS) distributions. At the local level, we evaluate cross-relation geometric consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages. Results show that global geometry is structured strongly by the context POS across all representations. Locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations, while immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially, highlighting different usages. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based representations, with cross-method agreement varying by relation. These findings demonstrate that dependency-conditioned embeddings exhibit systematic global linguistic organisation alongside relation-sensitive local lexical structures, with the extent of geometric consistency varying across representation methods.

candidates.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
candidates.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7 percentage points and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.

candidates.title: Kameleo: In-Situ Activation-Precision Selection for Bit-Serial LLM Accelerators
candidates.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps the activations of large language models (LLMs) in a higher-precision format, pushing the on-chip inference cost to the activation arithmetic. Bit-serial, variable-length accelerators offer a promising path to reduce this cost by lowering activation precision while preserving model quality. They process only the mantissa bits that each layer needs. The length has to be chosen per layer and operator, and today it is chosen by offline calibration: a search driven by the perplexity of the full model on a representative dataset. The search is repeated for every model and workload, and its result degrades silently on other data. This paper presents Kameleo, an accelerator that selects the activation precision at runtime, on the accelerator, from the data it is processing. Kameleo replaces the global perplexity by a local proxy that compares the output of each GEMM at reduced and at full precision. It exploits the fact that a bit-serial datapath produces this comparison almost for free, because the reduced-precision result is an intermediate state of the full-precision computation. Two passes over the first tokens of a workload set the precision of every GEMM. On four LLMs and seven datasets, Kameleo stays within a 1% perplexity budget at a 2.11-2.34x reduction of prefill cycles on the matrix multiplication unit (MXU), close to the reduction of configurations calibrated offline on the evaluation data itself. Calibrated configurations transferred to other data, in contrast, often violate the budget. The selection hardware adds only 3.7% to the accelerator area. Kameleo thereby makes variable-length mantissas feasible in real deployments, where offline calibration for every model and workload is not.

candidates.title: System-One RSI: Building Muscle Memory for Interactive Agents through Guided Practice
candidates.abstract: Reasoning models provide strong multimodal task understanding but struggle with sub-second control because deliberation increases decision latency. Fast decision models can meet the response window, yet prompting and few-shot examples do not readily provide the fine-grained experience required by a new task. Inspired by coached motor learning, this paper presents System-One Recursive Self-Improvement (System-One RSI), which couples two loops. The high-frequency online inner loop is an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) cycle: a decision model maps each visual observation and task question to structured judgments, and a decision tree converts them into timed actions without invoking a reasoning model. The offline outer loop is a recursive improvement cycle carried out by a team of reasoning agents. The team revises the decision-model prompt and decision tree, captures interaction records, derives supervision from those records, and trains or deploys updated model parameters. The improved system then returns to the environment and generates the experience for the next round, consolidating learned distinctions as external muscle memory. The framework operates with a small number of real episodes, without expert demonstrations, environment modification, sandboxing, or parallel simulation. Experiments in Snake, Zenless Zone Zero, and Black Myth: Wukong use a 27B decision model. Mean Snake score increases from 1.30 to 7.35. In an evaluated scenario of Zenless Zone Zero, median completion time decreases by 8.4%. In an evaluated combat scenario of Black Myth: Wukong, the evasive policy achieves 11 times the mean survival time of a stationary reference, while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7% across the evaluated configurations.

candidates.title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human--Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
candidates.abstract: Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes, while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release our implementation as open source to support reproducibility and adoption.

candidates.title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model
candidates.abstract: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.

candidates.title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
candidates.abstract: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.

candidates.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
candidates.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.

candidates.title: Understanding MoE Decisions Beyond Gradients
candidates.abstract: Understanding a language model's decision requires knowing how its internal computations affect its preference between answers. Gradient-based methods estimate this influence by predicting the effect of changing those computations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, replacing one expert can change which experts later layers select. Those switches can alter the answer scores in ways that derivatives do not capture. We introduce a predictor that uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate these extra effects, then adds them to a second-order prediction. Across questions from three benchmarks, our method reduces the error in predicting answer-score changes by 60\% on Qwen3.6 and 47\% on Gemma4, relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.

candidates.title: Learning to Compare Neural Representations from Parameterized Computation Graphs
candidates.abstract: Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.

candidates.title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
candidates.abstract: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.

candidates.title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
candidates.abstract: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.
